solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Leave father out

blocks.note: pop is an informal word for a dad
a light that is out is off

explanation.walkthrough: Read the surface as a family walking out on dad; in fact the two words after the definition simply sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: To pop off is informal British speech for going away quickly, so it can replace the verb in most sentences.

clue.text: God poisoned converts

indicators.note: a convert changes into something else, so the letters of the word before are changed into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: A deity has slipped something toxic to the people who switched faith to him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Converts' reads as a noun, the new believers; as a verb it tells you to rearrange the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Poseidon is the Greek ruler of the sea, one example of a deity from classical mythology.

clue.text: Stuffed, as the case may be — in this battle?

definitions.text: Stuffed, as the case may be — in this battle?

blocks.clueFragment: Stuffed, as the case may be
blocks.note: surface reading: a stock phrase meaning 'full up, depending on circumstances'
setter's reading: a cover for bedding, whose stuffed contents are the weapons in a playful bedroom scrap

explanation.walkthrough: 'As the case may be' is an idiom; here the case is the cotton cover around the soft thing you swing, and 'stuffed' is its filling.
explanation.definitionFit: The weapons in such a battle are feather-filled cushions in their cotton covers, swung by children at a sleepover.

clue.text: Sword, perfect fit

blocks.note: the light blunt blade used in fencing
a person or thing that complements another by contrast

explanation.walkthrough: A comedian's straight man is the classic example of the second sense: the partner who sets off the other perfectly.
explanation.definitionFit: Fencers use a light blunt blade of that name, and a contrasting partner who shows another off well is also called one.

clue.text: Christian, say, can always set upon Greek character

indicators.note: in an across answer, placing 'can' and 'always' upon the letter means they come straight after it

blocks.note: the Greek letter M
a can is a tin
e'er, the poetic contraction of 'ever'

explanation.surface: A believer who can always overpower a Greek.
explanation.walkthrough: Christian is not a believer but Fletcher Christian, who led the 1789 rebellion on HMS Bounty; 'say' flags him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Fletcher Christian seized the ship Bounty from Captain Bligh, making him the most famous example of a rebel sailor.

clue.text: Tulips on ground, immaculate

indicators.note: something ground has been crushed and broken up, so the flowers' letters are broken and remade

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: Spring flowers lying perfect on the soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like the earth the tulips sit on; it is the past tense of grind, and 'on' is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something in pristine condition, with no damage or blemish at all.

clue.text: Order spaghetti spoon, last bits taken with fork

indicators.note: the final bit of each of the two utensil words is all that is kept
taking one thing with another puts them together, so the kept letters join the word for a fork

blocks.note: the final letters of spaghetti and spoon
a fork in the road is where it splits

explanation.surface: A diner asks for pasta cutlery and eats the last mouthfuls with a fork.
explanation.walkthrough: The fork is not cutlery at all but a place where a road divides.
explanation.definitionFit: A court issues this as a formal command requiring someone to do or stop doing something.

clue.text: Bird featured in documentary running uphill

indicators.note: something featured in a film appears within it, so the letters sit inside the next word
in a down answer, going uphill means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters U-M-E sit in the middle of this word

explanation.surface: A nature film shows a flightless bird sprinting up a slope.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird really would appear in a wildlife documentary, so the surface is nearly literal.
explanation.definitionFit: The emu is a large flightless Australian species, an example of a bird.

clue.text: Cop out in Greene novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the author's name is made into something new

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters

explanation.surface: A police officer bows out in one of Graham Greene's books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' pretends to be one of Graham Greene's books, and 'Cop' pretends to be a policeman in it.
explanation.definitionFit: To back out of a promise or commitment is to go back on one's word, the verb sense of this phrase.

clue.text: Tubas etc, low musical range about right

indicators.note: to be about something is to go around it, so the low range goes around the letter for right

blocks.note: the lowest range of voices or instruments
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Tubas and the like have a low range that is about right.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is almost true: tubas do play in the bass range, so the wordplay hides in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Tubas belong to the orchestral section of metal wind instruments, and 'etc' widens them to the whole family.

clue.text: Regular bond has one committed

indicators.note: to be committed is to be put inside an institution, so 'one' is placed inside the bond

blocks.note: solder is metal used to join or bond
the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A steady relationship in which one partner is fully devoted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regular' looks like an adjective; it is the noun for a professional member of the standing army, as opposed to a reservist.
explanation.definitionFit: Regulars are full-time professional troops in a standing army, as distinct from volunteers or reservists.

clue.text: Stay sharp squeezing juice of orange and lemon, finally

indicators.note: the heads of 'juice' and 'orange' are taken, read as 'the J of juice, the O of orange'
to squeeze something is to hold it tight inside, so the word for sharp wraps around the juice letters
finally points to the very end of the citrus word before it, keeping one letter

blocks.note: a sharp taste is a sour one
first letters of juice and orange
the last letter of lemon

explanation.surface: A cook keeps a drink tart by pressing citrus into it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stay sharp' reads as an instruction to be alert; 'Stay' is the definition alone and 'sharp' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A sojourn is a temporary period of residence somewhere, the noun sense of a visit or stopover.

clue.text: Smooth seaweed rolled over

indicators.note: something rolled over is turned end to end, so the seaweed word runs backwards

blocks.note: nori is the seaweed wrapped around sushi

explanation.surface: Slippery seaweed tumbling over on the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smooth' looks like an adjective describing the seaweed; it is a verb, and sushi-rolling fits 'rolled' neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: To press creases out of cloth with a hot flat appliance is to make it flat, the verb sense of smooth.

clue.text: Hard to believe sun-god ain’t tanned!

indicators.note: to tan someone is to beat them, and beaten letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: An incredulous remark that the god of the sun has no suntan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tanned' fits the sun-god picture as a colour, but its job is the other sense, a thrashing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something so surprising it strains credibility is amazing or staggering, an adjectival synonym.

clue.text: Simply put, where kernel found?

blocks.note: an idiom for summing something up briefly
literally, the location of the edible seed inside its hard casing

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second half is taken literally: the kernel of a nut sits inside its casing.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means stated concisely and plainly, and literally names the casing that holds an edible seed.

clue.text: Old scientist shared mice out

indicators.note: letters let out run loose, so the shared mice scatter into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: An elderly researcher has let loose the lab mice he shared with colleagues.
explanation.walkthrough: The laboratory surface makes 'Old scientist' look like a character rather than the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Archimedes of Syracuse was a Greek mathematician and inventor of the third century BC, an ancient example.

clue.text: In the zone — and red-hot?

blocks.note: sporting slang for performing brilliantly
literally burning

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves can mean playing brilliantly; the second also works literally as burning, which is the double sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A player in top form is said to be performing brilliantly, and something ablaze is literally burning.

clue.text: Dull top hat

blocks.note: a dull performance is a flat one
a cap is a lid or top

explanation.surface: A drab top hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top hat' reads as one item; split it, and 'top' is wordplay while 'hat' alone is the definition. A flat cap is the soft peaked cloth cap of the British countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: The flat cap is a soft rounded cloth cap with a small brim, one example of headwear.

clue.text: Villain has stolen a fashionable company garment

indicators.note: a thief holds what he has stolen, so the villain word holds the three pieces that follow

blocks.note: a rat is a scoundrel
used as it stands
what is in is in fashion
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A crook has stolen a coat from a trendy clothing firm.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'fashionable company' a single brand; it is two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A waterproof coat for wet weather is one example of an item of clothing.

clue.text: Selfsame chum failing a lot

indicators.note: a failing friend is falling apart, so the letters of the pal word collapse into a new order

blocks.note: as in 'the very same', meaning identical
anagram fodder, 4 letters

explanation.surface: The same old friend fails often.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very' as an adjective means exact or identical, as in 'the very man I wanted', which is why it matches 'selfsame'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases work as adverbs of degree meaning greatly or to a large extent.

clue.text: Genius, he stuck in blunted knife, backwards!

indicators.note: a blunted blade has lost its point, so the knife word loses its tip at the end
the shortened knife is read from right to left
sticking something in puts it inside, so 'he' goes inside the knife word

blocks.note: a dagger is a short stabbing knife
used as it stands

explanation.surface: A brilliant man stabbed himself with a dull blade, the wrong way round.
explanation.walkthrough: Cut the last letter of the knife word, turn what is left around, then put 'he' inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An egghead is an informal, slightly mocking term for a highly intellectual person, a brainy sort.

clue.text: Sound publication

blocks.note: loudness, as on a stereo knob
a book, one of a set

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound publication' reads as a reliable journal, with 'sound' meaning trustworthy; the answer uses its noun sense instead.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the loudness of audio and also a single bound book in a series.

clue.text: Therapist, having skipped a page, so happy, I gathered

indicators.note: to skip something is to leave it out, so 'a' and 'page' drop from the letters that follow
things gathered up are bundled together in no set order, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters before removal
'a' as it stands and P for page, both taken away

explanation.surface: A patient notes that the therapist, missing a page of notes, was cheerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I gathered' pretends to mean 'I understood'; 'gathered' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Physio is the British short form of physiotherapist, a clinician who treats injuries through exercise and massage.

clue.text: Land fish

blocks.note: to settle on a branch, as a bird does
a freshwater species

explanation.walkthrough: 'Land fish' reads like an instruction to an angler to bring in a catch; both words are definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird alighting on a branch settles there, and the same word names a spiny freshwater species.

clue.text: Another gem proving fake, dislike merchant?

indicators.note: a fake is not what it claims to be, so these letters are not in their true order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: A jeweller has been sold one more counterfeit stone and wonders if the dealer is to blame.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is playful: a monger is a dealer, as in fishmonger, so a dealer in dislike stirs up hatred; the question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: A monger trades goods, so someone who peddles enmity and stirs up prejudice is jokingly a trader in it.

clue.text: See vampire bats slip away last of all

indicators.note: 'of all' means from every one of the four words, and 'last' keeps each one's end

blocks.note: the final letters of the four words

explanation.surface: Watch vampire bats slink off into the night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last of all' sounds like 'finally' in the story; it means the end of every word.
explanation.definitionFit: To espy is to catch sight of something, a literary synonym for spotting or glimpsing.

clue.text: Tethered by groom, a retired horse

indicators.note: a thing tethered by others is held fast between them, so the letters are held within the next words

blocks.note: runs across the end of 'groom', 'a' and the start of 'retired'

explanation.surface: An old horse, put out to pasture, tied up by the stable hand.
explanation.walkthrough: Groom and horse share a stable, which disguises that 'groom' is only a letter source.
explanation.definitionFit: A mare is an adult female of the equine species, so it is one kind of horse.

clue.text: Keep embroidering things, reportedly for little devil

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than read, so the phrase for continual stitching counts by its sound

blocks.note: to keep stitching is to stitch on and on

explanation.surface: Someone keeps stitching items for a mischievous child.
explanation.walkthrough: Repeating a verb with 'and' shows something done over and over, which is why the stitching phrase means to keep at it.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling a rascal a so-and-so is a mild euphemism for a stronger insult, much like calling him a little devil.

clue.text: Mountain pass left alone, initially, when climbing

indicators.note: the start of each of the three words is kept, the rest dropped
in a down answer, climbing means the letters go from bottom to top

blocks.note: the opening letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A mountaineer leaves the pass behind and climbs alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mountain pass' reads as one thing; 'Mountain' is the definition and 'pass' is only a letter source.
explanation.definitionFit: An alp is a high peak, especially in Switzerland, so it is a type of mountain.

clue.text: Drink and drink with posh wine-maker

blocks.note: cha is British slang for tea
a common drink
U means upper-class in British usage

explanation.surface: Drinking a lot in the company of a smart vintner.
explanation.walkthrough: The two drinks are the same beverage in different words: cha is old British slang for tea. U, for upper-class, is a standard crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: A French wine estate producing its own vintages is named for its castle or manor house, as in Bordeaux.

clue.text: Facing work, ask about it

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so the word for ask goes around 'it'

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a work
to pose a question is to ask it
used as it stands

explanation.surface: Confronted with a job, enquire about it.
explanation.walkthrough: OP for opus is a musical work number, a common crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Two houses across the street from each other are situated face to face, the positional sense of the word.

clue.text: Bloke tripped over, alack!

blocks.note: someone who tripped over fell down
both are cries of regret

explanation.surface: A man stumbled and cried out in dismay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' belongs with 'tripped' and does not signal a reversal here. Bloke is British slang for a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Fellah is an informal spelling of fellow, a casual word for a man or guy.
